title: Akrura bows in the dust
hookLine: Kamsa's messenger rides to Vraja full of longing, and rolls in the dust of Krishna's footprints
carry: devotees bow to the dust he walked
tomorrow: what do the gopis do when the chariot leaves?

cards: A chariot is on the road to Vraja, and its driver is carrying a trap. King Kamsa of Mathura has learned that the cowherd boy everyone talks about is the son he was warned of, the one born to kill him.
So Kamsa plans a festival: a contest of wrestlers, and an elephant at the gate. All he needs is someone the boys will trust to bring them. He chooses Akrura, a respected elder of their own clan.

teach.h: THE KING'S MAN, AND KRISHNA'S DEVOTEE.
teach.b: Here's the surprise. Akrura is Kamsa's messenger, and Krishna's devotee. The Bhagavata spends the whole ride inside his head, and what's there isn't dread.
It's longing. All the way he turns one thought over: I'm going to see him. Will Krishna look at him kindly, or hold him at arm's length as the king's man?
He reaches Vraja at sunset, as the cows come home.
In the dust of the cow pen he sees footprints, and knows whose they are; the text says they carry the marks devotees look for on the soles of Krishna's feet.
Akrura jumps down from his chariot and rolls in that dust, overcome. Then Krishna and Balarama come out to meet him. No arm's length.
The brothers embrace him, take his hand, lead him in, wash his feet and feed him.

Krishna asks after his family, and only then asks what brought him. And Akrura, the king's messenger, tells them everything: Kamsa's hatred, the festival, the plan. Krishna and Balarama laugh, and agree to go.
Akrura's bow in the dust is a moment devotees treasure.
A well-known verse in the Krishna tradition names one great devotee for each of bhakti's nine ways, and Akrura is its model of vandanam, bowing in prayer. And the dust became holy too.

Pilgrims to Vrindavan still touch the dust of Braj to their foreheads, and some go around Govardhan bowing full length on the ground, because Krishna walked there. The road was the king's errand. The bow was Akrura's own.

how: Akrura is remembered by devotees as a model of vandanam, bowing in prayer; pilgrims to Vrindavan touch the dust of Braj to their foreheads, some circle Govardhan bowing full length, and the chapters of Akrura's journey are recited at katha.

games.q: you're Akrura, arriving in Vraja at sunset with the king's summons. in the dust you see Krishna's footprints. what do you do?
o: jump down from the chariot and roll in the dust.
hurry on to deliver the message.
games.why: Akrura leaps from his chariot and rolls in the dust of the footprints, overcome. tradition makes him the model of vandanam, bowing in prayer.

practice: Many Hindus begin the day by touching the floor and then their forehead, and bow at the feet of elders the same way: a small vandanam. Try it now.
Touch the ground, bring your hand to your forehead, and think of a place where God has felt near to you. If you pray, bow there in your mind, the way Akrura bowed in the dust of Vraja.
If you don't, touch the floor and thank one place, or one person, that has held something good for you.

wordCard.voice: Leaving Vrindavan. The turn in the Bhagavata when Akrura comes from Mathura with Kamsa's summons, and Krishna agrees to go.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: Vrindavan, the forest of Krishna's childhood among the cowherds.
